articles.title: Patrick Mahomes Shares Positive Update on Knee After Week 6 Win
articles.summary: Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes gave an update on state of his knee after the team's win against the Los Angeles Chargers. The post Patrick Ma...
articles.body:
The Kansas City Chiefs remain undefeated in the 2026 season, having beaten the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 6 to go 5-0.

The Chiefs are the only unbeaten team in the AFC, alongside the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings make up the only teams to have not been bested yet in the NFL.

Perhaps the even more impressive note to the Chiefs' win-streak is the fact that quarterback Patrick Mahomes is coming off a serious knee injury back in December that saw him tear his ACL and LCL in his left knee.

Patrick Mahomes Speaks on Knee Health After Chargers Win

Mahomes was ready to start the year after making a quicker-than-expected recovery, and five games in has looked his best self in the regular season in almost half a decade.

Speaking to the media after the win against the Chargers, the former two-time MVP shared how his knee was feeling as he continues to get closer to 100%.

"After the bye week, I felt better physically… There's still some burst I don't have… But that's something we'll continue to work on." Mahomes said after the game, via Charles Goldman.

Patrick Mahomes 'Better' Despite Not Having Full Burst

Even though the 31-year old has been practicing since training camp and has yet to miss a game this season, his words make it clear that being on the field does not inherently imply a full bill of health in the National Football League.

The exact timeline for Mahomes getting his burst back to what it was prior to the injury is unknown. And for players sustaining serious knee injuries after the age of 30, there is no guarantee he'll ever be quite as fast as he was before.

But him feeling improved and is certainly a positive for the team, and whilst Mahomes is an agile QB, him having game-breaking speed has never been major part of his game.

articles.title: ‘The Gap’ in the WSL remains – but creating competition takes time
articles.summary: Good news first: it’s definitely shrinking. It being ‘The Gap’. The Gap being the space between the Women’s Super League’s entrenched top three and the rest....
articles.body:
Good news first: it's definitely shrinking. It being 'The Gap'. The Gap being the space between the Women's Super League's entrenched top three and the rest.

It is, though, assailable by pre-match face painting and savvy coaching and, if you're Birmingham City, who snagged a point off Arsenal on Saturday, Oceane Hurtre's left foot.

Of course, The Gap is still there if you're, say, Tottenham Hotspur or Brighton & Hove Albion, the former having suffered a 6-2 defeat to Chelsea before the latter fell 3-2 to Manchester City.

The result leaves Spurs with just two wins from 54 matches played against the WSL's top four (Chelsea, City, Arsenal and Manchester United), Chelsea claiming 13 wins from 13. While Brighton can boast two wins from their 13 meetings with City, Sunday was not one.

"After the first three goals, it was a bit like, 'Wow, are we that good and they are that bad?'" said City head coach Andree Jeglertz after his side's 3-2 victory. "Of course that's not the reality. If you drop a couple of percentages in this league, teams are good enough to punish you. Brighton is this type."

Jeglertz knows this. Brighton were one of only three teams to beat City last season to make their inevitable WSL title lift feel, for a brief moment, not so inevitable. Of course, City still lifted the trophy, handed Brighton a 4-0 defeat in the FA Cup final a month later and walked away Sunday with all three points as Brighton slumped to 10th.

But it's time for one of WSL's annual rituals: arguing whether this is the most competitive season to date, whether our collective patience and relentless hounding of head coaches regarding The Gap's existence and their plan to conquer it has finally coalesced into its closing.

Since the 2014-15 season — when Liverpool clinched the title ahead of Chelsea and Birmingham City finished third — the triumvirate of Chelsea, Arsenal and City have occupied the top three spots on all but two occasions, when Manchester United crashed in at second and third in the 2022-23 and 2024-25 seasons respectively.

This does nothing to blunt our enthusiasm each season, firing questions about The Gap like fevered confetti at those teams squatting on its wrong end. What's the plan this time, guys? Have you considered trying a pre-match DJ? Manchester City have a pre-match DJ. And £1.6million per year to pay Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw, who scored twice against Brighton.

Chelsea have eight league titles, a wage bill of nearly £15m as of 2024-25 and Lauren James, who also scored twice on Sunday. Arsenal do bottomless brunch. They also have decades' worth of infrastructure and history, plus women's football's first £1m player. Not their fault you don't, of course. But do you do bottomless brunch?

"Look, they didn't build what they've built in 15 months," head coach Martin Ho said ahead of the trip to Chelsea. "We'll get there, but we have years of work to do."

What Ho said is important. It's also important what he didn't say, the unenchanting euphemism skulking in the corner. "But you can't say that," one WSL executive, speaking anonymously to protect relationships, tells The Athletic .

"That" is the years of investment that women's teams are expected to make up in a matter of seasons, by ingenuity and passionate partnerships and letting fans take pints to their seats and appointing managers like Ho. Or, if you're London City Lionesses who currently sit third in the WSL table after their 2-1 win against Everton, hiring a matchday brass band. Plus spending at least £2.4million on transfer fees across two seasons and recruiting four players in the summer with nine Ballon d'Or Feminin nominations between them, including two-time winner Alexia Putellas.

This isn't some grim requiem for the game. It's not even a critique. Rather, it's the uncomfortable but necessary starting point for any conversation about The Gap.

This season has cut a compelling argument for its shrinking. According to Opta, non-big four sides averaged 0.42 points per game against the traditional big four before this weekend, the highest on record across a season since 2015 (0.43). This is in line with steady and increased investment by all clubs, almost all of which have broken their record transfer fees in the space of 18 months.

Yet, context is important. Arsenal are unexpectedly suffering their worst-ever start to a WSL season . United's jagged start boiled down to the appointment of a new manager just two weeks before the season's start. Hurtre's goal against Arsenal, coupled with one in the 3-1 defeat to Manchester City last month, represented the first time in WSL history that a promoted side scored against either team at first attempt, a reminder of just how gargantuan the gap was to begin with and remains. In the season's sixth week of fixtures, United, City, Chelsea and London City all comfortably saw off opposition by an aggregate score of 14-6.

That women's football harbours a deep desire to close The Gap isn't unique. This is the preoccupation of competitive sport, if not modern existence. How much bootstrap pulling is required here? What optimisations have we not considered?

At which point we should cast our eyes to the league next door, the one swamped in its own financial ruin, wondering who has the hose. Yes, we're talking about Manchester City's men's team, but all the rest of it too: the 94 per cent of men's clubs that lost money last season, the nearly two-thirds of English Football League and National League clubs that are technically insolvent , the more than a quarter in the top five divisions that would run out of cash within the lifespan of a fruit fly if their owners pulled the plug.

This should be a neon red sign for women's football. Almost all WSL sides remain financially dependent on their parent company, according to last season's financial records. Yet, salaries and transfer fees continue to fatten, despite revenue and attendances failing to keep up. Many clubs could be at risk of contravening the league's new financial rules come season's end.

Clubs investing seriously in their women's and girls' setups should be encouraged. The evidence is the fact that with each season, we ask about The Gap, more galvanised as the inches chip away.

Yet elite sport is inherently stratified. While breaking through is the thrill, we should be wary of cajoling teams to bridge the gap too quickly, to manoeuvre in manners that are unsustainable, that mimic mistakes elsewhere.

"The scoreline is obviously damaging," Ho said post-match. "But if you'd asked me whether we could push Chelsea as much as we did in that first 60 minutes, compared to 15 or 16 months ago, people would've probably said no."

articles.title: Combined match review: RSL earns second road victory of, Royals fall at home
articles.summary: In both the win and the loss, Royals and RSL players see milestones reached
articles.body:
Utah Royals FC fell 2-0 at America First Field against the Kansas City Current on Saturday evening in front of 10,809 fans, the club's second-highest attendance this season. Unable to secure the victory, the squad will now be forced to wait yet another week to officially clinch its first playoff berth in club history.

While the Royals were unable to earn the result in the battle at home, Real Salt Lake traveled to Kansas City, earning a 3-1 victory to lift itself to a second road win in the 2026 season. The victory earned the visitors an important three points to keep the push for the postseason alive in the doubleheader evening for Utah professional soccer against Sporting Kansas City.

URFC sees Del Fava and Cronin Reach key milestones in 2-0 loss

As the Utah Royals took the pitch on Saturday evening the home side was without the heartbeat of its midfield as Japanese star Mina Tanaka was out due to a hamstring injury sustained while on international duty. URFC captain Paige Cronin earned an impressive milestone Saturday against the Current, starting in her 100th NWSL match.

Iron woman Kate Del Fava returned to the pitch following her USWNT debut as a second-half substitute in Tuesday's 2-2 draw against Spain. The defensive wall not only leads the Royals in possessional passes and clearances but, made her 80th consecutive start today, the longest active streak for a single club. Del Fava has played 7,661 straight minutes, the second longest streak in club history while also having played every one of the 7,211 minutes Utah has played as a team in 79 games since the Return to Royalty in 2024.

First career brace for Guilavogui helps to lift RSL to 3-1 victory

Real Salt Lake got off to a near perfect start against Kansas City to earn just its second road win of the 2026 MLS season with goals by French attacker Morgan Guilavogui and Spanish Rookie Sergi Solans in under 15 minutes. The score by the Frenchman in the 12th minute marked his third of his first MLS season, while 2026 RSL Golden Boot leader Solans netted an impressive 12th MLS goal of his rookie season to double the visitor's lead.

The hero through the first 10 minutes of the second half was undoubtedly 22-year-old Kobi Henry who headed a ball just before it crossed the goal line in the 53rd minute following an RSL turnover that found RSL goalkeeper Rafael Cabral out of position. In the 61st minute Guilavogui found the net again for his first career RSL and MLS brace, burying a ball off a perfectly placed assist by German metronome Noel Caliskan.

"I'm not too concerned (about the remaining games) actually, I think it's just the reality of continuing to do what we've been doing. I think we showed up as the Royals we are today and almost got a result as a team that is good, a team that has scored eight or nine goals in its previous two games." — URFC Head coach Jimmy Coenraets

"I thought the guys up front did a really good job probing behind the backline, the movement behind the backline opened up a lot of space between the lines and the decisions in and around goal were really good. Our midfield of Noel and Stijn were top and then our backline of Kobi, Phil and Luc helped us be dangerous on both ends." — RSL Head coach Pablo Mastroeni

While the home side opened up the match with pressure, earning scoring chances early, it was the visiting side that struck first, heading the ball into the net off a corner kick in the 21st minute. Although the Royals surged throughout the remainder of the first half in hopes of an equalizer, the mounting calls in favor of the Current, along with a 1v1 shot against URFC 'keeper Mandy McGlynn to nearly double the lead, left the home side down 1-0 heading into the break.

As the second half began the Royals continued in its pursuit of a goal with Cece Delzer narrowly missing a header just left of the goal before recently acquired forward Jameese Joseph entered the match in the 62nd minute immediately forcing the Kansas City keeper to make two saves off powerful shots just outside the box. In the 91st minute the visitors were able to double the lead after two prior goals were disallowed due to offside. Although URFC was unable to find the back of the net the home side continued to battle with grit and energy until the final minute of the match.

The lightning-fast start for RSL put a RSL side in dire need of earning points in front with a 2-0 lead just 14 minutes into the match. The goals by Guilavogui and Solans showcased a team working as one as each score had a beautiful buildup that multiple players were involved in to seamlessly work the ball up the pitch and throughout the offensive end to lift its attackers to two early scores.

Although the visitors took an early 2-0 lead, some defensive confusion led Sporting Kansas City to earn one back in the 26th minute. After the heroics of Henry in the 53rd minute RSL was able to ease the defensive pressure with Saba Lobjanidze bringing the ball up the pitch for 2026 World Cup standout JuanMa Sanabria, whose shot from the center of the box was stopped by the SKC keeper.

The second-half goal by Guilavogui not only showcased his precise shooting abilities, but, the goal line run and slot back by Caliskan was one of beauty, helping to give RSL more breathing room, with a 3-1 lead.

Utah Royals FC remain at home next Friday, Oct. 23 to face the Seattle Reign for its final regular season match of the 2026 NWSL season. Kickoff is scheduled for 7:30 p.m. MDT with tickets available on the Utah Royals website.

Real Salt Lake will round out the weekend of home matches for Utah soccer, welcoming St. Louis City SC to the Wasatch Front on Saturday, Oct. 24, with kickoff also at 7:30 p.m. MDT and tickets for that match are also available for purchase on the RSL website.

articles.title: Nashville SC Locks Up 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup Spot
articles.summary: Nashville SC is the first MLS club to clinch a spot in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup. The team has guaranteed a finish no worse than third in the league's...
articles.body:
Nashville SC is the first MLS club to clinch a spot in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup. The team has guaranteed a finish no worse than third in the league's overall standings, with matches still remaining on the 2026 schedule.

The math is simple: Nashville's position is now unreachable by any chasing club, even in a worst-case run to close out the season. That removes any dependency on other results and hands the front office an international fixture to plan around a year in advance.

Qualification doesn't end the ambition. Third place is the floor, not the ceiling, and Nashville still has reason to push for a higher finish before the playoffs begin. A stronger regular-season position carries weight heading into the postseason, where seeding and momentum matter.

The early clinch also gives the roster-building process a head start. Playing continental and domestic competitions at once demands depth — injuries, suspensions and fatigue all hit harder across a packed calendar — so locking in the Champions Cup spot now lets the front office plan accordingly instead of waiting on the regular season's final weeks.

The Concacaf Champions Cup is the region's top club competition, pitting MLS sides against teams from Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. For Nashville, it's a chance to test the squad against different styles and raise its profile beyond the domestic league — part of a broader push by MLS clubs to build credibility on the continental stage.

articles.title: Mbappe scores two, Guler one, as Real Madrid find form before El Clasico
articles.summary: Real Madrid beat Sevilla 4-1 a day after Barcelona thrashed Real Betis 5-2 as the Spanish giants prepare for El Clasico.
articles.body:
Kylian Mbappe scored twice as Real Madrid closed the gap on La Liga leaders Barcelona to six points with ⁠⁠a 4-1 win over Sevilla at the Santiago Bernabeu, a week before the rivals meet.

Despite the absence of suspended Vinicius Jr, Real produced the fluid attacking football the team had been lacking of late, with Arda Guler again orchestrating their best work on Sunday.

After a stale opening, the Turkish international sparked the match into life.

Sevilla appealed for a red card following an incident involving Guler and Peque Fernandez, but Guler responded minutes later by collecting Yan Diomande’s pass and arrowing a shot into ⁠⁠the top corner.

Mbappe scored an equally impressive second in the 37th ⁠⁠minute, turning brilliantly to burst through on goal before calmly beating Odysseas Vlachodimos.

Fede Valverde, restored to right back by coach Jose Mourinho, made a crucial block to deny Felix Correia just before the hour as Sevilla threatened to work ⁠⁠their way back into the contest.

Diomande then exploited the space created by Sevilla’s more adventurous approach, evading his marker before sending Mbappe in ⁠⁠behind the defence. Andres Castrin brought down the French forward, ⁠⁠who got to his feet to convert the resulting penalty and effectively settle the contest.

Substitute Manu Bueno reduced Sevilla’s arrears with a composed finish 10 minutes from time after Mbappe cheaply surrendered possession deep inside his own half.

Diomande restored Real’s ‌‌three-goal advantage two minutes later, capping a fine display with a thunderous strike.

Eder Militao received a warm ovation when he came on in the 85th minute for his first appearance since undergoing ‌‌hamstring ‌‌surgery in April.

Mourinho will take encouragement from one of the most complete performances of his second spell at Real as they prepare for next Sunday’s pivotal meeting with Barcelona.

Real, who have won three straight games in all competitions following the international break, climbed ⁠⁠to third on 21 points, one behind Atletico Madrid, while Sevilla are sixth on 14.

Earlier on Saturday, Barcelona beat Real Betis 5-2 to make it nine wins from nine and ⁠⁠stretch their blistering league tally to 39 goals.

Lamine Yamal lit the fuse with a dazzling opener before Rodri, Gabriel Jesus, Eric Garcia and substitute Dani Olmo joined the party, while Valentin Gomez and Ez Abde replied for Betis, who played much of the ⁠⁠second half with 10 men after Facundo Bernal was sent off for head-butting Lamine.

Barca moved to 27 points, five above Atletico, who won 1-0 at Espanyol, while third-placed Betis have 19 and Real Madrid sit fourth on 18 before welcoming Sevilla on Sunday.

Elsewhere, Osasuna withstood second-half pressure from Racing Santander to win 2-0 in Jagoba Arrasate’s first game back as manager.

Two flying saves from Ionut Radu denied Alaves a point in a 2-1 defeat to Celta Vigo, while ‌‌Real Sociedad won 5-2 at Malaga.

articles.title: Tony Pulis column: Beer & Blackpool beach was how British players bonded
articles.summary: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains what Spurs will get from their team-bonding trip to Spain, and how differently managers built team morale in his day.
articles.body:
Hearing about Tottenham 's team-bonding trip to Marbella last week made me think about the similar methods I used as a manager to build team morale.

While some things have changed from my day, the idea behind taking your players away to a new environment where they will benefit from spending a lot of time together has not.

I wrote a few weeks ago about how Spurs boss Roberto de Zerbi needed time with his players on the training pitch after their poor start to the season, to bed them in and build a proper team.

He will have used their warm-weather camp in southern Spain to do more of that, getting to know what is almost a new squad of players.

With De Zerbi being cut from Italian cloth, I am sure the players will have been working mornings and afternoons to drill in the manager's principles in respect to team shape and direction.

But that's not the only purpose of taking them away. De Zerbi will also have been able to monitor the different personalities within the group away from the grass.

If the trip has worked then, as well as getting them ready to face Coventry on Monday night, I am sure he will now, for the first time, understand the strengths and weaknesses of each individual, on and off the field.

'I found out a lot about them - good and bad'

A few eyebrows were raised about Spurs going away so early in the season but it makes perfect sense to me when you consider so many new players arrived there this summer, with several signings late in the transfer window.

When I was Stoke manager, I often took my teams away to Austria in our pre-season for the same reasons De Zerbi and Spurs have gone to Spain.

Those trips were set up not only to test the players' fitness, but also to see how the group worked together.

I have always believed in building a family togetherness within the dressing room, with a commitment from every player to the benefit of the team.

The extreme tests that we asked our players to do over that 10-day period brought out an inner determination to fulfil the tasks given them and, in my opinion, helped us through some tough times early on in our Premier League campaigns.

Watching the lads slowly bond together on the training pitch and at meal times was great to see and I found out a lot about all of them, good and bad.

Yes, I have to admit one or two players were short of the character we wanted and needed, but they didn't last long and left with no bad feelings on my side.

Beer & Blackpool beach - what British players classed as bonding sessions

Today, whether it's pre-season or a winter break, most Premier League clubs who take their players away go first-class and enjoy great hotels, great facilities and wonderful food.

Wherever the team bus goes, it is followed by an even bigger bus with all the non-playing staff on it.

It is very different to my experiences in my early years as a player, when we would be taken to Blackpool for three days' pre-season training.

Again, the idea was to bring the lads closer together, but that happened in a different way than today's professionals are used to.

We stayed in a guest house with three-quarter beds that we all shared - that certainly brought us closer together! - then trained on the beach each morning, doing our running sessions on the sand.

Then we played seven-a-side games in the afternoon on a local park pitch, after clearing the dog muck off first.

In the evenings, we were allowed out for a few beers, with no time stipulated for our return - apart from having to be downstairs and ready to hit the beach again at 8am the next morning.

That is where things have changed most of all, right through football, during the past few years. In the 1970s and 80s, there was a massive drinking culture right through the leagues - just listen to the stories that came out of clubs as big as Liverpool , Manchester United or Arsenal , when they had teams who not only dominated English football but the European game too.

In my early years of management, the bonding I've been talking about used to happen right through the season through the lads meeting in pubs after games and after training on week days as well.

Winter breaks were rare and, rather than for a training camp, the only time most players I knew went to Spain was at the end of the season when more alcohol would be consumed.

That was what British players classed as bonding sessions and, as I've written about before, even the ones at the top level were much more connected to normal society, rather than living in an eternal bubble.

Now, while they are certainly more aware of the dangers of drinking to excess, as a manager you have to find other ways for them to connect when there are other distractions to contend with.

One item I am very glad my generation was not brought up with is mobile phones. I used to go mad if I walked into a dining room at the training ground or a hotel to see a group of lads looking at their phone and not engaging with each other.

I sometimes think that, as a young player, I had nothing compared to the players of today but, really, we had everything.

The stories, the friendships and the memories of the togetherness I remember from every dressing room during that time still resonate with me and recreating them was always my aim as a manager.

Some other things have changed too - I am not sure De Zerbi has ever considered taking his team away to an army camp like I did on many occasions early in my managerial career, where we worked on the players in different ways.

One year, I took Stoke down to Exmouth, where the lads were put through their paces doing cross-country circuits.

That probably doesn't sound too bad on the face of it, but it was freezing cold and chucking it down and the circuits incorporated climbing and swimming under water in a darkened tunnel - I did all of it too by the way - while trying to keep up with the Army PT Instructor.

That was just the morning, the afternoon was spent indoors, where the boys were set different kinds of tasks, where their minds were tested with more practical team-building exercises where they had, say, 20 minutes to use some drums and planks to cross an area without touching the ground.

At night, they slept in bunk beds with only plastic sheeting over the mattress, and one very thin blanket.

Like my own trips to Blackpool as a player, it was spit and sawdust but everyone bought into it and attacked every challenge with great gusto and spirit.

As I moved onwards and upwards as a manager I was allowed to take teams abroad, to locations that were a little more lavish.

Irdning in Austria is my favourite destination, and somewhere I have taken many clubs over the years.

It is a small town in the Alps that is ideal in every aspect of what I wanted as a manager, and not just because of the mountains I made my players run or cycle up!

We have almost always stayed in the same place there, too - a 1,000-year-old building I call 'The Castle'. It has swimming pools, a large gym, saunas, steam rooms, a spa and a golf course - you get the picture.

Real Madrid stayed there all the time too - it led to us playing them in a friendly in 2007 because we had already booked it and they said they would play us if we swapped hotel - yet my first time there could have turned out to be a disaster.

It was in 2004, during my first spell as Stoke manager, when I was having a tough time under the Icelandic ownership who were at the club at that time - I liked them as people but we all tended to largely disagree when it came to football.

My first-team then was made up of some really strong characters, but who were also great lads and old-school to the core, in the ways I've been talking about in this column.

During our first three days in Irdning, they had worked their socks off. The fourth day was meant to be the rest day where, fishing, golf or shopping was on the agenda but the players had other ideas.

Gerry Taggart, who was a fantastic lad, came and asked if the boys could borrow the team bus and go somewhere to have a few beers away from our hotel.

Now, being a manager and not in the dressing room as a player, my responsibilities had changed. The group had been brilliant in responding to all the hard work I had thrown at them, so I agreed - well, kind of!

Knowing what a 'fun-loving' group the lads were, and the fact they would be out of my sight, and control, the alarm bells were going off in my head, loud and clear.

So, without the lads' knowledge, I paid the bus driver a few quid to make sure he didn't find any really exciting places, and they ended up coming back to the hotel.

The players eventually worked out that I had instigated this under-cover plot but I know it didn't stop them having a great time because it was at our hotel, where I could keep an eye on them.

That's probably not something De Zerbi had to worry about last week!

I wanted to end this column by talking about a football match.

Manchester City 's Champions League game against Paris St-Germain last week was an absolute throwback, which provided so many crosses, shots and goalmouth action.

PSG were fantastic in the first half but City really showed their teeth after the break and, in my humble opinion, were unlucky not to get anything out of the game.

Both teams played football through the pitch, got the ball to the most talented players - the forwards - as quickly as possible and produced unbelievable excitement.

There was no passing backwards or square, and hopefully any young coaches watching will have been influenced by both teams' urgency to play forward.

You cannot mention City at the moment without referencing what is going on with them off the pitch.

When news broke that they had been found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules, I wrote tongue in cheek, asking City to send over the FA Cup and winners medals from 2011 to my old club Stoke.

Surprisingly, they have not arrived... but as the fall-out continues from the verdict of the independent commission, I'd like to add some further thoughts on the whole saga and ask some questions of my own.

Football has not been the winner and the whole game has been soured by this story, not just the Premier League.

But one thing I would like to ask people to explore is why, after the Premier League discovered that City first broke these rules, it has taken so long get to this point.

Why were the Premier League top-brass still standing on the podiums, presenting City with the many trophies they have won in this time? The situation now has cast a shadow over the entire game.

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

articles.title: La historia interminable del Sevilla en el Bernabéu
articles.standfirst: Otro arbitraje salpicado de polémica y la pegada del Real Madrid acaban con la imbatibilidad de los hispalenses a domicilio
articles.summary: Otro arbitraje salpicado de polémica y la pegada del Real Madrid acaban con la imbatibilidad de los hispalenses a domicilio
articles.body: Decía Michael Ende acerca de La historia interminable que para descubrir la realidad hay que atravesar el filtro de lo fantástico, aunque siempre con el riesgo de que la propia fantasía pierda su contenido. En las visitas del Sevilla al Santiago Bernabéu en los últimos años sucede un fenómeno parecido, pues el marco que rodea a estos partidos está tan condicionado por las presiones mediáticas a los árbitros que logra beneficiarse de esa misma situación que se denuncia. Y cuando todo se convierte en un "estás conmigo o contra mí", el análisis futbolístico prácticamente carece de sentido. La derrota por 4-1 frente al Real Madrid no se explica solo desde la pizarra, sino desde una inercia que perpetúa los 18 años de sequía nervionense en la capital. Respecto al once que jugó con el Levante, las ausencias de Kochorashvili y Miguel Sierra propiciaron la entrada de Peque y Rubén Vargas, que no jugaban desde la tercera y la primera jornada respectivamente. La inclusión del mediapunta catalán obligó a Fofana a retrasar su posición y acompañar a Agoumé en la medular. Incluso desde el doble pivote, el jugador cedido por el Milan presionó muy alto, dibujando a veces un 4-1-4-1. A pesar de las bajas, el Sevilla salió al césped sin complejos con la pelota, manteniendo su fútbol vertical y minimizando riesgos en los primeros compases del choque. El duelo en el Bernabéu se caracterizó por las decisiones de la sala VOR, donde Cuadra Fernández no consideró oportuno corregir a Busquets Ferrer en dos acciones determinantes. En el minuto 20, en un ataque de los blancos, Peque agarró a Güler de la camiseta y este le respondió con un codazo deliberado en el rostro sin balón de por medio. Una agresión evidente que el VAR ni siquiera mandó a revisar. Así empezó la paradoja de una noche donde la grada de animación desplegó una pancarta que rezaba "no es fútbol, son Tebas y Negreira", generando ese ambiente de victimismo que pone en la diana al colectivo arbitral. Si el primer gol fue obra de Güler poco después de ser perdonado, el 2-0 marcado por Mbappé estuvo precedido de una falta previa de Konaté a Robbie Ure que tampoco fue revisada. Más dudoso resultó en la segunda mitad el penalti de Castrín sobre el delantero francés, pero ratificó que las decisiones caigan siempre del mismo lado. "Sabíamos a lo que veníamos", dijo Juan Iglesias al término del encuentro, mientras su entrenador, Luis García Plaza, se mostró más tajante: "En la Liga a veces juegas partidos en superioridad o inferioridad y hoy nos tocaba hacerlo en superioridad; con 0-0 teníamos que jugar 65 minutos once contra diez, ese es el resumen del partido". En lo estrictamente táctico, el Sevilla prescindió de ese trivote rocoso que le había funcionado en las últimas jornadas. Peque ofreció mayor clarividencia con pelota en la zona de enganche, pero tanto Fofana como Agoumé se vieron desbordados y el sistema se tambaleó en fase defensiva debido al alto ritmo del juego. Sin ese tercer hombre de contención, el Madrid encontró autopistas para correr con espacios, favorecido por un bloque muy concentrado y solidario sin balón donde se percibe el sello inconfundible de José Mourinho. La vulnerabilidad de la medular hispalense quedó al descubierto en la jugada del 1-0. En una rápida transición de Diomande -el mejor futbolista del partido-, ni Fofana ni Agoumé acompañaron el repliegue, permitiendo que Güler recibiera con libertad en la frontal para armar el disparo que adelantó a los locales. Por cierto, la gran actuación del extremo marfileño supuso la noche más difícil para Juan Iglesias en lo que va de curso. La estructura del Sevilla ganó equilibrio y solidez tras el paso por los vestuarios con la entrada de Manu Bueno. El canterano, un centrocampista más puro y con más trabajo sin balón, le dio al equipo mayor capacidad para apretar en campo contrario y no perder las vigilancias. Además, su presencia elevó el nivel de Agoumé y liberó de cargas defensivas a Fofana, permitiéndole dar un paso al frente y empujar el bloque varios metros más arriba para complicar el inicio de juego al conjunto blanco. Vargas actuó de inicio por derecha buscando meterse por dentro para generar superioridades. Sin embargo, el suizo aún está lejos de su mejor nivel. En el descanso, la entrada de Ejuke le dio otro aire al ataque. En medio del debate planteado en la previa sobre quién debe relevar a Miguel Sierra por la derecha, el nigeriano demostró que sabe utilizar sus virtudes desde cualquier perfil: agobió a Cucurella, amenazó continuamente a la zaga madridista y generó espacio para que Juan Iglesias se proyectara en ataque, protagonizando entre ambos los mejores minutos de los suyos. "Nos hemos rebelado, hemos tenido situaciones buenas para marcar y metimos gente de refresco que ha estado acertada. Manu ha marcado el gol y ha estado muy bien, Ejuke ha desbordado mucho y Lucas ha entendido bien el juego", analizó Luis García Plaza, que eligió bien a los hombres que salieron del banquillo. Precisamente Manu Bueno y Stassin fabricaron la jugada del 3-1, ayudando a que el Sevilla haya anotado en las nueve jornadas disputadas hasta la fecha. Ya en el tramo final, con el partido encarando sus últimos veinte minutos, García Plaza había aprovechado para retirar del envite a Juan Iglesias y a Félix Correia -ambos con tarjeta amarilla- para dar entrada a Carmona y Alfon, esta vez por izquierda. De esta forma, concedió el primer descanso de la temporada al lateral vallisoletano, que venía jugándolo todo. Un doble movimiento pensando en la gestión de minutos y en la próxima cita ante Osasuna en Nervión. Tras la enésima derrota del Sevilla en el Bernabéu, García Plaza reflexionó sobre la polémica que salpica al estamento arbitral en LaLiga: "Los que más se quejan son los que menos se tienen que quejar: Madrid, Barça y Atlético. Llevo mucho tiempo en esto y es siempre la misma historia". Resulta bastante irónico que el club blanco alimente el relato de una competición viciada mientras los nervionenses siguen atrapados en un bucle cada vez que visitan su estadio. Por más que cambien los actores, el guion siempre parece escrito de antemano. El Sevilla se marcha de la capital con la cabeza alta y un gen competitivo innegociable. Si bien tiene apenas un punto más que el año pasado a estas alturas, ya ha digerido las tres citas más complejas de la primera vuelta liguera, prolongando sus buenas sensaciones y terminando la jornada en sexta posición. Ahora le toca convertir la indignación por los arbitrajes del Ciutat de València y el Bernabéu en el carburante perfecto para reencontrarse con la victoria ante su público.

articles.title: El Cádiz pierde la paciencia con Celades
articles.standfirst: El club comunica la destitución del técnico catalán, que solo ha sumado siete puntos de 30 y que deja al equipo en zona de descenso a Primera Federación
articles.summary: El club comunica la destitución del técnico catalán, que solo ha sumado siete puntos de 30 y que deja al equipo en zona de descenso a Primera Federación
articles.body: El Cádiz ha agotado su paciencia con Albert Celades. El consejo de administración ha comunicado este lunes a primera hora de la mañana la destitución del entrenador, que deja al conjunto amarillo en puestos de descenso a Primera Federación después de sumar siete puntos de treinta posibles. La derrota del domingo en Granada ha sido el último golpe de una etapa que ya comenzó de forma abrupta y que ha terminado sin encontrar los resultados. La salida alcanza también a Raúl Valbuena y Juan José del Ojo, que cesan en sus funciones. El club ha agradecido el trabajo de los tres y les ha deseado suerte en su futuro profesional, sin anunciar todavía quién asumirá la dirección del equipo. Celades había aterrizado en una situación complicada, ya que sustituyó a Imanol Idiakez cuando faltaban cuatro días para comenzar la liga y tenía por delante una plantilla profundamente renovada tras los 17 fichajes realizados. Sin pretemporada para implantar sus ideas, el técnico empezó a construir mientras competía, pero el calendario avanzó más rápido que las victorias. El 4-0 al Leganés hace un par de jornadas pareció ofrecer un punto de partida y, sobre todo, de inflexión para el técnico. El Cádiz encontró fútbol, goles y una conexión con la grada que invitaba a pensar en un cambio de dinámica. Nada más lejos de la realidad. Fue su única victoria. Porque después llegaron los dos golpes definitivos para el técnico. Primero, el Sporting se llevó el triunfo del Nuevo Mirandilla con un tanto en el minuto 87. Después, el Granada resolvió el derbi andaluz con los goles de Gumbau y Jorge Pascual tras el descanso. El entrenador había defendido la evolución del grupo, especialmente en el apartado defensivo, aunque él mismo admitía antes de visitar Los Cármenes que esa mejoría no bastaba. La clasificación ha terminado imponiéndose. articles.title: El Cádiz alcanza un acuerdo verbal con Borja Jiménez para su banquillo
articles.standfirst: El técnico abulense, de 41 años y actualmente en el Al-Ahli catarí, será el próximo entrenador cadista si nada se tuerce
articles.summary: El técnico abulense, de 41 años y actualmente en el Al-Ahli catarí, será el próximo entrenador cadista si nada se tuerce
articles.body: El Cádiz y Borja Jiménez han alcanzado un acuerdo verbal para que el técnico se haga cargo del equipo. Si nada se tuerce, el entrenador abulense será el próximo inquilino del banquillo gaditano, aunque el entendimiento todavía está pendiente de formalizarse. Borja Jiménez, de 41 años, dirige actualmente al Al-Ahli de la Qatar Stars League, al que llegó el pasado 3 de julio. En sus seis encuentros ligueros al frente del conjunto catarí ha sumado dos victorias, un empate y tres derrotas, con un balance de siete puntos. Su llegada al Cádiz supondría su regreso al fútbol español después de su etapa en el Sporting de Gijón durante la temporada 2025-26, en la que dirigió 37 partidos. Antes estuvo dos campañas al frente del Leganés, con el que conquistó el título de Segunda División. Su trayectoria también incluye los banquillos de Deportivo, Cartagena, Asteras Trípoli, Mirandés, Rápido de Bouzas, Izarra y Valladolid B. Con licencia UEFA Pro y el 4-2-3-1 como sistema preferido, Borja Jiménez es el elegido para asumir el equipo cadista, a falta de que el acuerdo verbal se convierta en definitivo. El Cádiz ya ha despedido a Albert Celades tras sumar siete puntos de 30 posibles y dejar al equipo en puestos de descenso a Primera Federación. El técnico, que llegó cuatro días antes del inicio liguero a una plantilla con 17 fichajes, solo ha logrado una victoria, el 4-0 ante el Leganés, y las posteriores derrotas frente al Sporting y al Granada precipitaron su salida junto a sus ayudantes Raúl Valbuena y Juan José del Ojo. El club busca una reacción inmediata y Borja Jiménez, actualmente en el Al-Ahli catarí, figura entre los principales candidatos para ocupar el banquillo. Si nada se tuerce, él será el próximo entrenador.

articles.title: Mou agita el avispero
articles.standfirst: Los dos últimos partidos han permitido ver la versión más intervencionista del luso, tanto desde el banquillo como desde el once
articles.summary: Los dos últimos partidos han permitido ver la versión más intervencionista del luso, tanto desde el banquillo como desde el once
articles.body: El Real Madrid llega al partido del domingo en Barcelona con el viento de cola de dos victorias con consecuencias diferentes. Los tres puntos de Roma le permiten mantener el pleno en la Champions. La victoria del domingo, en cambio, mantiene una desventaja importante con relación al líder de la Liga, una situación que puede cambiar en caso de éxito blanco en Cataluña. Los dos triunfos del Madrid, con un total de ocho goles anotados, llevan el sello más personal de José Mourinho, que ha intervenido decisivamente tanto desde los cambios, como ocurrió en la capital italiana, como a partir de la confección del once inicial. Ante el Sevilla, el entrenador del Madrid tomó decisiones de peso, justo lo que se esperaba de él cuando se acometió la operación de su retorno al Madrid. Dos movimientos fueron determinantes. Primero, la alineación de Fede Valverde como lateral derecho, un cambio que empieza a ser un clamor en amplios sectores de la afición. Esa decisión deshace la pareja del uruguayo con Tchouaméni, que hasta el momento ha dejado más dudas que certezas, y además potencia una posición en la que ni Trent ni Dumfries acaban de enamorar. La segunda decisión de Mou fue colocar a Arda Güler en el doble pivote. Un cambio al que el propio entrenador se resistía en los primeros partidos de la temporada, ya que veía (y sigue viendo) al turco más determinante cerca del área. Pero las evidentes carencias del equipo en la zona de creación hicieron que el técnico rectificara, y el equipo lo agradeció. El fútbol mejoró y Güler tuvo incluso impacto directo en el mercador con el primer gol de los blancos al Sevilla. El tercer cambio fue 'obligado', aunque todo apunta a que será uno de los debates de la temporada. Con Vinicius sancionado, el extremo izquierdo fue para Yan Diomande, que firmó seguramente su mejor partido como jugador del Madrid. Finísimo en el regate, el marfileño creo un sinfín de situaciones de peligro, aunque casi todas se malograron en el último pase. Un aspecto sin duda a mejorar por parte de Diomande, que a cambio firmó un buen gol para cerrar la cuenta del Madrid. Un tanto al que se sumó una asistencia, segunda consectiva tras la de Roma, datos que dibujan el impacto creciente del ex del Leipzig en el ataque del Madrid. El renovado once ante el Sevilla llegó cuatro días después del partido de Roma, en el que el Madrid remontó una desventaja de dos goles para acabar ganando el partido en los últimos 10 minutos. Mou planteó ante su ex equipo un once más académico, pero no dudó a la hora de revolucionar el planteamiento tras el 3-1. La salida del campo de Dumfries, sustituído por Güler, reordenó al equipo, con el turco directo al eje y Fede bajando al lateral, la misma fórmula empleada este domingo en el Bernabéu. Además, cambió a Tchouaméni por Bernardo y acabó llenando el once de jugadores de ataque, con las salidas de Endrick y Espì, ambos decisivos para la remontada. El brasileño se ganó un puesto en el once ante el Sevilla, pero su impacto fue menor que el que protagonizó en el Olímpico, donde fue una tortura para la defensa romanista. En resumen, dos partidos ganados con dos intervenciones decisivas de José Mourinho desde la pizarra. Para esto le fichó el Madrid, en busca de un revulsivo táctico que por fin parece haber llegado al Bernabéu.

articles.title: Duncan Ferguson: Ex-Everton and Rangers striker named manager of Irish Premiership club Glentoran
articles.summary: Ex-Everton and Rangers striker Duncan Ferguson is named as the new manager of Irish Premiership club Glentoran.
articles.body:
Former Everton and Rangers striker Duncan Ferguson has sensationally been named as the new manager of Irish Premiership club Glentoran.

The 54-year-old, who also played for Dundee United and Newcastle United and won seven caps for Scotland, will take up the reins at the east Belfast club on what the club say is a "multi-year contract".

Ferguson's coaching career to date includes being assistant manager at Everton under renowned managers Carlo Ancelotti and Rafael Benitez, and also two spells as caretaker boss.

In recent years, he has managed Forest Green Rovers and Inverness Caledonian Thistle.

Ferguson's surprise appointment follows the departure of Declan Devine as manager of the Irish League outfit in September.

His former Dundee United team-mate Gary Bollan, with whom he worked at Inverness, has been named as assistant manager.

Glentoran have not won a league title since 2009 despite significant investment from owner Ali Pour and the adoption of a full-time professional model in recent years.

"I am delighted to become manager of Glentoran," said Ferguson, whose first game as boss will be at home to Ballymena United on Saturday (15:00 BST).

"This is a big club with a tremendous history, and it is a great opportunity for me. I understand the responsibility that comes with the job.

"I want to win trophies here. Glentoran should be challenging for the title and every cup and shield we enter. I know that success here will be judged on what we win.

"The more I spoke with Ali and Paul [Millar, sporting director], the more I wanted the job. Their ambition matches my own, and I am looking forward to getting onto the training pitch, working with the players and seeing what we can achieve together."

What awaits Everton hero Ferguson in shock Glens role?

Ferguson link has caused a 'real buzz' - McCann

Glentoran net late to snatch win against Limavady

'We took the time this decision deserved'

Ferguson, who also worked under Roberto Martinez and Ronald Koeman at Everton, added that he has "signed for the long term".

"I want to get to know the people at the Club and in the wider community and become part of life here. That is important to me," he said.

"I have heard so much about the Glentoran supporters and what this Club means to them. We have a responsibility to win games and make them proud. Their support has to be earned, and I am looking forward to getting started."

Glens owner Pour said Ferguson's appointment reflects the club's "ambition to win trophies".

"We took the time this decision deserved. We conducted a rigorous recruitment process, interviewing candidates from across the United Kingdom, Ireland and Scandinavia," added Pour.

"We carefully assessed their experience and proposals and completed our due diligence before making the appointment.

"Paul and I met Duncan on several occasions in Liverpool. Those conversations gave us the opportunity to explore his approach to management, discuss the demands of the role and understand what he could contribute to Glentoran.

"His football knowledge, experience and determination to take on this opportunity impressed us. Duncan demonstrated the qualities we were looking for in coaching, leadership, player development and recruitment, supported by strong relationships across the game."

Former Glentoran captain Paul Leeman, who played 597 games for the club, is excited at the prospect of Ferguson in the Oval dugout.

"I still can't believe it - it's a huge appointment and I'm interested to see his plans for Glentoran," Leeman told BBC Radio Ulster.

"It is a risk and he's been known more as a number two. But he has bags of experience in football. He's worked at the top, top level and there's certainly something he can add to the team.

"He doesn't know the league so I think he has to have people around him who do.

"He's coming to the Irish League to probably try to resurrect his own managerial career. He will demand respect from the players straight away and it's certainly going to be interesting."

The Glens had been linked with a move to appoint former Northern Ireland international Jim Magilton, but the ex-Ipswich Town and Queens Park Rangers boss opted to remain with their Irish Premiership rivals Cliftonville.

Devine left by mutual consent after two and a half years at the helm.

The former Derry City and Bohemians boss guided the club to a County Antrim Shield success in the 2024-25 season, their first trophy triumph since lifting the Irish Cup in 2020.

Ferguson is now tasked with ending the long drought since the Glens' last league victory 17 years ago.

Glentoran sit third in the Irish Premiership standings, having won six and lost four of their first 12 league outings this season.

articles.title: Scottish Premiership: Celtic step up against Hearts, Rangers slip up as Hibernian's woes continue under Marink Reedijk
articles.summary: Celtic eased to a 7-1 win against Hearts; Rangers drew 2-2 at Dundee; Hibernian lost 2-1 to Falkirk; Kilmarnock beat Motherwell 3-2; St Mirren lost 3-1 at Aberdeen; St Johnstone won 1-0 at home to Dundee United
articles.body:
Back-to-back defeats for new Hibernian boss Marink Reedijk means they are now bottom, while Motherwell and St Mirren could be in trouble after five straight defeats.

Celtic's lead at the top is now four points, the same as the gap between seventh and 12th.

We take a look at some of the talking points from another dramatic weekend of Premiership action...

Celtic had no wins in five, but went on an unbelievable scoring spree against last season's runners-up Hearts to extend their lead at the top.

Encouraged by their second-half showing in Thursday's 4-1 Europa League defeat to Benfica, the manager started with the front three that finished that game in Lisbon.

And all three - Benjamin Nygren, Callum Osmand and Camilo Duran - scored in the 7-1 demolition of their title rivals.

There was no place in the squad for Sebastien Tounekti after a dismal showing in Lisbon and Sunday's performance suggested O'Neill does have better options.

Celtic were outstanding at times but Hearts, who had lost just one of their last 14 games in all competitions, played a part in their own humiliation.

A failure to defend corner kicks was their undoing, losing two goals from Celtic's first three set-pieces.

The game was effectively over after 10 minutes, but by half-time the hosts had scored five.

Sky Sports' Kris Boyd accused the Jambos of showing Celtic a "lack of respect" adding it should be a "wake-up call" if they want to be real title contenders.

Boyd saw signs of Celtic under Ange Postecoglou, but can they hit the same levels for the rest of the season?

It is back to the Europa League and Benfica again for the Hoops on Thursday night, while Hearts are away to Trabzonspor in the Conference League.

Rangers went to Dundee knowing an eighth straight win would see them return to the top of the Premiership, at least until Celtic played.

But a poor first half and a late mistake from Dan Neil saw them leave Dens Park with a 2-2 draw.

They did work hard to undo a struggling start to take the lead, but one lapse in concentration from Neil saw them drop two points.

Derek McInnes said pre-match that it was too early to put pressure on their title challengers with a win, then claimed Dundee's second goal was like "a balloon popping."

There is no doubt it was an opportunity missed for the Ibrox side, and the manager will be keen for an immediate response when they host newly promoted St Johnstone on Saturday.

Reedijk can have no doubts about the size of job he has inherited at Hibernian after his home debut ended with them dropping to the foot of the table.

It is now six league games without a win for the Easter Road side, who are in great need of a goalscorer.

They can attack, but lack that final touch in front of goal.

Combine that with too many needless errors and it is clear to see why the Hibees are looking up at the rest of the league after nine games.

The fans are demanding an immediate improvement, but next up is the daunting challenge of Celtic on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

They also have a massive League Cup semi-final clash against Edinburgh rivals Hearts on November 1. Can the new boss turn things around before that trip to Hampden Park?

Pressure mounting at Motherwell and St Mirren?

It looked like Alfred Johansson had picked up where Jens Berthel Askou left off at Motherwell, but five straight defeats means the Fir Park side are just one point from the foot of the table.

They are now on their longest losing run since February 2025, as the side who were brief title contenders last season find themselves in early trouble.

There were some positives and glimpses of the Steelmen of last season. Tawanda Maswanhise hit the crossbar, but they were sloppy and struggled to dominate against a side that had won just once going into the game.

Johansson needs to find some form and quickly. Their next challenge is a home clash against a hurting Hearts side who will also be desperate for a response.

St Mirren have also lost their last five Premiership games, but sit two points above Motherwell in eighth.

They started brightly against Aberdeen, but failure to take advantage of their first-half dominance cost them all three points.

Buddies boss Craig McLeish can take some positives from the first half at Pittodrie, but knows he has to halt their dismal run to avoid the possibility of dropping bottom of the table.

articles.title: Notre Dame on Cusp of Missing CFP and 8 Overreactions after Week 7 of 2026 College Football Season
articles.summary: When the dust settled and the final game finally ended well after midnight, the picture came into focus. Week 7 of the college football season delivered one of the most exciting and meaningful Saturdays the sport has ever seen.
articles.body:
When the dust settled and the final game finally ended well after midnight, the picture came into focus. Week 7 of the college football season delivered one of the most exciting and meaningful Saturdays the sport has ever seen.

This isn't an overreaction. This is a proper reaction.

With an avalanche of upsets—including absolute madness inside the top 10 of the AP Poll—the greatest sport on earth just reminded the world how unpredictable it can be.

As we approach Halloween, the stakes grow higher. The schedule grows shorter. The race to the end of the season picks up steam. As it does, our overreactions grow more robust.

Needless to say, after the madness that was, we have plenty to work with. Overreact we shall.

After Saturday, it's abundantly clear that we don't have a dominant team in college football in 2026.

We have good teams. Heck, we have great teams. But there is not a team that feels unbeatable in the sport, and Saturday showcased this in a historic way.

The No. 1, No. 2, No. 5, No. 6 and No. 7 ranked teams in the AP Poll lost in Week 7. Big favorites lost, unbeatens lost, small favorites lost.

There were losses everywhere, and we will cover many of them at length.

We've spent the last few weeks trying to figure out the truly exceptional teams across the sport. The only team that looked like it might have fit that mold was Georgia, especially after such a strong win over Alabama on the road. On Saturday, the Bulldogs lost outright to Auburn at home 27-24 despite coming into the game as roughly a three-touchdown favorite.

Woof. And not the kind of woof for the Bulldogs.

The national championship chase has never been less clear, and that should make for a thrilling homestretch.

College Football Has a Sesimic Officiating Issue

Too often this year, the officiating has been the story rather than the teams, players and coaches. And after Week 7, we once again find ourselves dissecting what the refs should have done (or didn't do) rather than the games themselves.

One could argue that the officials in the Notre Dame-BYU game missed two key plays. First, there was a clear defensive pass interference at the end of the game that was missed. More concerning is the fact that the officiating crew ended the game, even though there should have been one second remaining.

The Big 12 released a statement late on Saturday night confirming as such, essentially confirming that Big 12 officials botched this final moment that gifted BYU a 28-24 victory.

This season alone we've already seen enough. There was the Michigan-Western Michigan Hail Mary to kick things off, which featured clock malpractice similar in nature. We missed a flag on Tennessee's illegal dropkick against Texas and also had an incorrect spot on Oregon's two-point conversion try against UCLA.

Oh, it's a tough job. But botching huge moments with replay available—especially when it comes to something like clock time—is unacceptable.

The stakes are too high for teams to lose the way Notre Dame did. Simple as that.

It has to be better, or we start to question the integrity of the whole operation.

Officiating Aside, Notre Dame is a Miami Loss Away from Missing the CFP

Notre Dame's 28-24 loss to BYU was indeed controversial, and we'll be thinking about what could have been for quite some time.

That acknowledged, it won't change the result. Notre Dame's schedule is no longer unblemished, and the team's remaining path doesn't exactly ooze excellence beyond one game moving forward.

The good news? That one game is a good one. Notre Dame plays Miami in November, and it will take place in South Bend. If there are doubts about this team, the Irish can silence them in short order.

The bad news? The schedule is largely "meh" outside of two games, which is how Notre Dame has operated in recent years.

The best win to date came against Wisconsin in Week 1, and the Badgers are coming off a loss to UCLA. Beyond that, the Irish play SMU, which has played better of late, but that doesn't jump off the page.

A win over Miami and a clean finish solves these issues. No debates. No weirdness. No selection committee questions But a loss at home, regardless of what else transpires, and things could easily turn (again).

A 10-2 season with this schedule might not be good enough.

Notre Dame fans don't want to hear it after last year, but a scenario is taking shape yet again.

Biggest Disappointments of 2026 CFB Season 😞

Ohio State's Quarterback Situation Will Ultimately Sink This Team

Julian Sayin was injured in the second half of Ohio State's wild 19-15 win over Indiana, and his immediate future is somewhat unknown. (We hope he gets healthy soon.)

Ryan Day told reporters that Sayin would be out "several weeks" following the game, although there will be more clarity on that in the days to come.

The Buckeyes have a bye next week, which couldn't come at a better time. After that, they'll travel to USC, play Oregon and Northwestern at home and then travel to Nebraska.

All of these games are supremely winnable under normal circumstances, although this isn't exactly normal.

While he's out, true freshman Luke Fahey and former 5-star Tavien St. Clair will compete for reps. Needless to say, there's plenty of concern. The lack of experience at the position could spell problems, especially if Sayin is out for a prolonged period.

It's also fair to question if Ohio State should have done more in the transfer portal to add depth and experience to that position, but that ship has sailed.

The bigger picture isn't a whole lot prettier. Sayin had some rough moments against Indiana, and he hasn't exactly progressed in a way many, including this writer, thought he would. While Jeremiah Smith has covered up a lot of QB worries, this was not a good day for the position and the outlook moving forward.

There were concerns before the injury; now those concerns are massive in scale.

The SEC Continues to Play its Way Out of the Playoff

In terms of parity and excitement, the SEC delivered. From a playoff perspective, however, no conference was dealt a bigger blow on Saturday than the SEC.

The conference came into the week with four teams ranked inside the top 10. Three of those teams lost. And Missouri, which came into the week ranked No. 13, was absolutely blown out by Ole Miss.

In terms of overall shock value, Georgia's defeat against Auburn was significant. When it comes to the impact on the College Football Playoff, however, Alabama's loss to Tennessee and Texas' wild loss to Florida could be the most impactful.

While one loss won't boot a team from playoff contention, three losses have historically removed teams from consideration entirely. That could change this season, of course, although a precedent has been set.

The SEC now has no unbeaten teams, and four teams have one loss. With so many massive games still to be played, the conference continues to deliver on the entertainment front. At the same time, it's been a brutal stretch for CFB Playoff resumes.

His facial expressions after the game said it all.

Following back-to-back losses against Oklahoma and Florida—games Texas was favored in by more than a touchdown—Steve Sarkisian couldn't hold back on his frustrations, saying all parts of the program will be analyzed.

Given how ugly it was at times in the 27-24 defeat, it makes sense. But in looking at the state of Texas, we should probably start to look at the head coach as well.

Sarkisian was paramount in bringing Texas back from the dead. The program is in a much better place than it once was, and his influence is a big part of that.

But it feels like the program has hit its ceiling, and Sarkisian's commitment to quarterback Arch Manning, at least to date, likely hasn't helped. Overall, the vibes surrounding the program just feel off.

Sarkisian's buyout is reportedly north of $50 million , and it's unlikely the Longhorns would do anything drastic this year. But this is how the hot seat conversation starts, and when it does, it becomes difficult to swing momentum back in the other direction.

Backup QB and All, UCLA is Trending Toward the CFP

While the SEC continues to stack losses, UCLA still doesn't know what that feels like in 2026.

In his first season with the program, head coach Bob Chesney is working miracles. The Bruins are 6-0, and they just beat Wisconsin 17-7 without starting quarterback Nico Iamaleava, who is out for the year with an injury.

Backup QB Ty Dieffenbach wasn't perfect, although he was good enough. And he showed enough to start considering how far UCLA can take this unlikely surge.

The schedule moving forward is remarkably favorable, which is perhaps putting it mildly.

UCLA only has two road games remaining, games at Minnesota and at Michigan. Outside of that, Chesney's team plays Michigan State, Nevada, Illinois and USC.

Of all the surprising things the 2026 season has delivered, UCLA's resurgence is near the top of the list. As the season grows deeper, however, the Bruins are on the cusp of morphing from a good story to a legitimate postseason threat.

The 24-Team Playoff Won't Kill College Football

We're breaking protocol some, expanding to the topic currently engulfing the sport. But no piece of news throughout Week 7 was bigger than this one.

A 24-team College Football Playoff is coming, and it's coming next season barring something unforeseen. Conference championship games will be gone, the playoff will add multiple rounds, and the sport will look drastically different one calendar year from now.

The general response from this announcement has largely been negative, and that makes sense. It will certainly change the sport we know and love.

But this won't kill college football. It won't kill the regular season. The postseason, which will occupy much more time than it once did, will still absolutely deliver, especially with more games being played on college football campuses.

Is it perfect? Goodness no. Did we need it? Absolutely not.

But the sprint to declare the sport dead each time a change is made has grown exhausting.

Everyone take a deep breath. It'll be fine. Saturdays will still be exceptional, and don't let anyone tell you otherwise.

articles.title: Arsenal were spooked by Brighton defeat and have reverted to type - they won't beat Bayern Munich, says Paul Merson
articles.summary: Sky Sports' Paul Merson pens his latest column on Arsenal's attacking issues following their narrow win over Nottingham Forest; Arsenal face Bayern Munich in the Champions League on Wednesday; Eberechi Eze's struggles continue in the Premier League
articles.body:
It frightened them and they've reverted to type. And the type is that they won't let in any goals, and they'll make an opportunity to score a goal, and that's exactly what they did at Nottingham Forest.

I don't think I've ever seen a game where a team has that much possession and still doesn't look like scoring a goal in a month of Sundays. It was as bad as it gets.

It's unbelievable how you can have that much of the ball and not look like scoring. I used to watch Arsene Wenger's teams and they would have 30 shots from that amount of play.

Other teams have seen the blueprint to play against Arsenal: sit back and defend. It's not hard. It's not like they're going to make 20, 30 chances. The wingers don't go past anybody. No one runs beyond the ball. The ball isn't being held up. There's no real movement.

I was blown away watching their performance against Forest. I know they won by not playing well, and that's a great sign, but at the same time I thought the shackles would be off this season and they would really start playing. Bruno Guimaraes has got to play in every game. He's the one who can pass the ball.

I just can't see how they beat Bayern Munich this week. If I was Bayern, I'd just open the game up and just say you have a shot, we have a shot because there'll only be one winner. Can Arsenal outscore teams?

This is a massive football match. This gives you a marker for where you are in the Champions League, because you just don't know how strong these leagues are.

I like Kai Havertz. He's a good footballer. But when the Bayern Munich centre-halves go to bed, is he giving them a sleepless night? Are they awake worrying that they're playing against Havertz?

X factor is what wins a Champions League and I don't see that at Arsenal. I don't see Havertz or Viktor Gyokeres as the difference-maker.

It's fine when you're playing against lesser teams, but it's different when you're playing against Europe's big boys. I still see Arsenal winning the league because I just think they just need one goal. I feel Manchester City need two goals every football game to win. Arsenal just need one and they'll win.

I've played for big teams and I've played for teams that weren't big - it's a different game. Eberechi Eze is a prime example. It's so, so different.

He was substituted at half-time against Forest, but if he played like that for Crystal Palace, he would still be on the pitch.

You've got to perform at Arsenal. You've got to play in a shape. You can't just play your own game. You can't be a free spirit at big clubs anymore.

At Palace, the team talk is 'give the ball to Eze, everything goes through him and then we'll work from there'. You go to Arsenal, there are four of them. Give the ball to Bruno. Give the ball to Bukayo Saka. Give the ball to Martin Odegaard. Give the ball to Declan Rice.

At Arsenal, he gets on the ball, and he's got to make things happen in the 25, 30 times he's touched the ball instead of the 100 times he touches the ball at Palace.

I've seen him try to nutmeg people on the edge of his own box at Crystal Palace and lose the ball, but it's alright. That's no disrespect to Palace, but it's just different playing for a big team.

The pressure is on week in, week out at Arsenal. They can win at Forest and they'll still get criticised by people like me. That's the difference.

I remember Aston Villa away last year. Eze falls asleep at the far post, Matty Cash scores and he gets subbed at half-time. He started only one league game in the next two months.

The lad can play. He's a lovely player, but I don't know if he'll be lovely for Arsenal. I don't know if he'll get the chance because as soon as he doesn't do well, he's off.

Arsenal have too many players on the bench, so it's easy to take him off. That's the problem.

articles.title: Luis Enrique: "No hay un equipo que sea perfecto"
articles.standfirst: El entrenador del PSG se rinde en elogios al Barça de Flick, pero insiste que hay más rivales para ganar la Champìons
articles.summary: El entrenador del PSG
articles.body: Luis Enrique es uno de los grandes protagonistas del gran duelo entre PSG y Barcelona de Champions de mañana en el Parque de los Príncipes. Con el de mañana serán ya cuatro duelos ante su ex club, dos en un cruce de cuartos que se saldó a su favor más el de la campaña pasada en la liguilla con triunfo en el Camp Nou. El entrenador ha vuelto a elogiar al Barça y no ve una final anticipada. No ha querido opinar sobre los graves incidentes de este fin de semana en Francia pero espera que mañana la gente disfrute solo con el fútbol. Si es una final anticipada: "no porque es la competición que nos permite jugar este tipo de partidos, somos de los favoritos pero hay más equipos que pueden ganar esta competición", Si disfruta con el PSG: "estoy orgulloso, claro, por cómo disfrutan mis jugadores, por la identidad y la personalidad del equipo en general. Es bonito verles disfrutar". Si espera algo de sus jugadores ante el Barça: "estos partidos son diferentes, son los de más alto nivel, adoro ver al Barça como entrenador y como aficionado. Es muy bonito ver esa identidad y creo que nos parecemos. Pero hay que saber que será un partido complicado porque son fuertes a nivel individual y como equipo. Pero no espero más de los jugadores porque hay que superar todos los problemas desde el colectivo". Los incidentes en París, si afectan: "no, no soy la persona para hablar de este tema. Estoy para hablar de fútbol, aunque a nadie le gusta la violencia". La baja de Nuno Mendes y Lamine Yamal: "la mejor manera de defender a Lamine es tener el balón, que no lo tengan ellos, para defender a un equipo con jugadores de calidad hay que superarlo con el equipo". Defectos del Barça: "no hay un equipo que sea perfecto. Tenemos la confianza para medirnos al Barça. Es un gran desafío". Qué le toca a hacer el fútbol tras lo visto este fin de semana: "tengo mi opinión, muy clara, pero no soy el indicado. No me preocupa la seguridad en el partido y espero que se pueda jugar el partido en las condiciones habituales". Vitinha dice que PSG y Barça son ahora los mejores junto al Bayern ahora mismo: "Si lo dice Vitinha es así. Pero hay más, está el City, el Arsenal, el Real Madrid. Esto de los mejores se verá en abril". Su famosa frase de adn Barça, si ahora sigue teniendo más adn: "¿pero acerté entonces? Sois tan buenos haciendo análisis, dime pues si acerté. cómo te cuesta eh (le dice al periodista). Nada, déjalo estar. Soy socio, fui jugador y entrenador seis años, tengo una relación increíble con Catalunya, mi familia son catalanes, antes me costaba enfrentarme al Barça pero ahora me empiezo a acostumbrar. Veo siempre al Barça, es el club que tiene unos valores muy claros que yo amo, no pegan una patada, son deportivos, pero soy del PSG y me gustaría ganar mañana. Es el club en el que me he sentido más importantes y es especial enfrentarme siempre al Barça". Elogios a Flick: "casa perfectamente con el adn Barça, que es atrevido, que vayas a ganar siempre, lo está haciendo de forma maravillosa y ahí están los resultados". Si Lamine, como dijo Guardiola de Messi, es imposible de marcar: "Creo que Lamine quiere ser Lamine y lo está haciendo muy bien y comparar al mejor jugador de todos los tiempos... ahí no va a ganar nadie. Veremos en el futuro, pero mejor no compararse".
